items.title: [qs] qs : qs.stringify with arrayFormat 'comma' throws an uncaught TypeError on array elements carrying a non-callable own toString (DoS)
items.summary: Summaryqs.stringify(obj, { arrayFormat: 'comma' }) throws an uncaught TypeError: Cannot convert object to primitive value when an array in obj contains an element that carries an own, non-callable toString property (for example { a: [ { toString: 'x' } ] }). A remote, unauthenticated attacker who can influence an object that the application later re-serializes with the comma array format triggers the throw. In a service that lacks a synchronous error boundary around the serialization call, the uncaught exception crashes the worker process, producing a denial of service.Root CauseWhen arrayFormat: 'comma' is selected, the comma branch collapses the whole array into a single value via Array.prototype.join, or, under encodeValuesOnly: true, maps each element through the value encoder before joining. Both paths perform an implicit string coercion (ToPrimitive with hint "string") on each element. For an object whose own toString is a non-callable value, coercion skips the shadowed non-callable toString, falls through to Object.prototype.valueOf (which returns the object rather than a primitive), and throws. The comma branch runs this coercion before the per-element null and skip handling in the main loop, so nothing downstream can neutralize the hostile element, and the throw is never caught inside the library.lib/stringify.js  (comma-array branch)  line 152-154: obj = utils.maybeMap(obj, function (v) { return v == null ? v : encoder(v); });  // encodeValuesOnly path  line 156:     objKeys = [{ value: obj.length > 0 ? obj.join(',') || null : void undefined }];   // default comma pathlib/utils.js  line 292:     string = String(str);   // value encoder coercion reached via the encodeValuesOnly pathImpactPrerequisites: the application calls qs.stringify with arrayFormat: 'comma' (a documented, supported option) on an object whose shape can be influenced by attacker input. Attacker-controllable sources include qs.parse(input, { allowPrototypes: true }), which retains a toString segment (Express 4's default query parser, Express 5's extended query parser, and body-parser's extended urlencoded parser all set it), qs.parse(input, { plainObjects: true }), whose null-prototype elements throw even without a toString key (eg, a[][b]=c), and JSON.parse of a request body, which needs no qs parse option at all. No authentication or user interaction is required. Demonstrated capability: a single request forces an uncaught synchronous TypeError in the serialization call. In a naive single-process Node service with no synchronous error boundary, this crashes the process and takes the service offline (availability impact). Under a framework such as Express that traps synchronous handler throws, the plausible outcome is a per-request 500 rather than a full outage; that lower-impact case is noted but not the worst credible supported deployment. There is no confidentiality or integrity impact, no memory unsafety, and no prototype pollution.Proof of ConceptInstall qs at the affected version (for example 6.16.0) and run the following script with Node.js. No network setup is required; it demonstrates the throw in isolation.var qs = require('qs');// Source A: qs.parse with allowPrototypes retains the hostile toString segmentqs.stringify(qs.parse('a[0][toString]=x', { allowPrototypes: true }), { arrayFormat: 'comma' });// Source B: a JSON request body, no qs parse option neededqs.stringify(JSON.parse('{"a":[{"toString":"x"}]}'), { arrayFormat: 'comma' });// Also affected: the encodeValuesOnly sub-pathqs.stringify(JSON.parse('{"a":[{"toString":"x"}]}'), { arrayFormat: 'comma', encodeValuesOnly: true });A default-join (allowPrototypes) => THREW: TypeError: Cannot convert object to primitive valueB default-join (JSON.parse) => THREW: TypeError: Cannot convert object to primitive valueC encodeValuesOnly path => THREW: TypeError: Cannot convert object to primitive valueN2 callable toString => NO THROW; output="a=z"N3 isBuffer vector (CVE-2026-82417) => NO THROW; output="a%5Bconstructor%5D%5BisBuffer%5D=x"qs version: 6.16.0Attack ChainExposure: A remote, unauthenticated request reaches an endpoint whose handler eventually serializes attacker-influenced data with qs.stringify(obj, { arrayFormat: 'comma' }).Control: The attacker supplies data that becomes { a: [ { toString: <non-callable value> } ] }, either via a[0][toString]=x parsed with allowPrototypes, or via a JSON body {"a":[{"toString":"x"}]}.Path: In stringify, the primitive/buffer guard at lib/stringify.js:134 is false for an array, so control reaches the comma branch at lib/stringify.js:149.Guard: On the encodeValuesOnly path, the closure v == null ? v : encoder(v) at lib/stringify.js:152-154 passes only null/undefined through; a non-null object still reaches the encoder. The default path skips that closure entirely and reaches obj.join(',') at lib/stringify.js:156 with no guard at all.Primitive: The element is coerced to a string (Array.prototype.join, or String(str) at lib/utils.js:

items.title: [undici] undici WebSocket client vulnerable to Denial of Service via failed HTTP/2 handshake
items.summary: Impactundici's experimental WebSocket client (enabled by default via allowH2: true) crashes the Node.js process when it connects to a malicious server over HTTP/2. If the server answers the WebSocket upgrade with a response that fails handshake validation, undici aborts the request, but the abort is a no-op because the request is already marked completed, so the underlying ClientHttp2Stream is left open with no error listener. When the server then destroys the connection, the orphaned stream emits an unhandled error and the process exits. A remote, unauthenticated server can therefore deny service to any client that opens a WebSocket to it over HTTP/2. undici 8.11.0 and 8.11.1 are affected; the regression was introduced in 8.11.0.PatchesUpgrade to 8.11.2.WorkaroundsSet allowH2: false to disable HTTP/2 for WebSocket connections, or avoid opening WebSocket connections to untrusted servers, until upgrading.Referenceshttps://github.com/nodejs/undici/security/advisories/GHSA-qq8j-7v2v-3rwphttps://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-109855https://github.com/nodejs/undici/pull/5873https://github.com/nodejs/undici/commit/dd28c5c55f4a25f7c441fd4365b1191f96c3b8bfhttps://cna.openjsf.org/security-advisories.htmlhttps://github.com/nodejs/undici/releases/tag/v8.11.2https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-qq8j-7v2v-3rwp

items.title: [@better-auth/drizzle-adapter] @better-auth/drizzle-adapter: Concurrent requests can exceed rate limits on PostgreSQL
items.summary: Am I affected?You are affected if you use @better-auth/drizzle-adapter from 1.6.17 through versions before 1.7.7 (including the 1.7.0 prereleases from beta.6 through rc.6) or @better-auth/kysely-adapter 1.6.17 through 1.6.31, and keep rate-limit records in a PostgreSQL database.All of these must be true:Rate limiting is enabled.Rate-limit records are stored in the database.The database is PostgreSQL, used through one of the adapter versions above.You are not affected if you store rate-limit records in memory (the default) or in secondary storage.SummaryDatabase-backed rate limiting on PostgreSQL can let a burst of concurrent requests go over the configured maximum. When many requests arrive at the same time, several of them can pass the limit check together. This weakens the rate limit on password sign-in, two-factor verification, one-time codes, password resets, and other rate-limited endpoints.ImpactAn attacker who sends many requests at once can make more attempts than the application allows.The issue does not bypass password or one-time-code validation. It does not directly compromise an account. The number of extra attempts is limited by the number of concurrent database connections, the number of application instances, and the rate-limit window.Patches@better-auth/kysely-adapter is fixed in 1.7.0. Upgrade to 1.7.0 or later.The Drizzle fix is merged for the planned @better-auth/drizzle-adapter 1.7.7 release. That package is not available yet. Upgrade better-auth and the installed Drizzle adapter together when 1.7.7 is available. No database schema or public API migration is required.WorkaroundsStore rate-limit records in secondary storage.Use a custom rate-limit storage that checks and increments the counter in one atomic step. An atomic step cannot be interrupted by another request.Enforce the intended limit at an upstream layer, such as a reverse proxy or gateway.In-memory storage also avoids this issue. However, each application instance keeps its own counter, so it may not enforce one shared limit in multi-instance or serverless deployments.Referenceshttps://github.com/better-auth/better-auth/security/advisories/GHSA-44jh-23m7-hpcfhttps://github.com/better-auth/better-auth/pull/11331https://github.com/better-auth/better-auth/commit/35d7cd389220f99cfc98ac699e6a42b48313a740https://github.com/better-auth/better-auth/releases/tag/v1.7.7https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-44jh-23m7-hpcf

items.title: [better-auth] better-auth: OAuth Proxy lets an attacker sign in as another user
items.summary: Am I affected?You may be affected if you use better-auth from 1.5.0-beta.12 through versions before 1.7.7 with the OAuth Proxy plugin. You are affected only if all of these are also true:On a participating environment, the OAuth Proxy plugin has no dedicated secret, or its secret equals that environment's global Better Auth secret.Sign-in state is stored in a cookie (account.storeStateStrategy: "cookie"). With a database or secondary storage, this is only the case if you chose it explicitly.Implicit account linking is on (the default).You are not affected by this path if every participating environment uses a proxy secret distinct from its global Better Auth secret, if sign-in state is stored in the database, or if you use a version before 1.5.0-beta.12.SummaryThe OAuth Proxy plugin trusts any user profile it can decrypt. In the affected setup, Better Auth encrypts sign-in state, including data the caller chose, with the same secret and hands it to anyone who starts a social sign-in. An attacker can use this to get a fake profile for another user's email address that the proxy accepts as real.ImpactAn attacker without an account who knows a user's verified email address can sign in as that user, with that user's permissions. They can read private data, change the account, and link a provider account of their choice to it. They need no provider sign-in and no action from the victim. No availability impact is established, and a reported open redirect was not confirmed.PatchesThe fix is merged for the planned better-auth 1.7.7 release. That package is not available yet.Upgrade all nodes handling the same cookie-backed OAuth or SAML state flow and all OAuth Proxy participants together, including the production coordinator and preview or development deployments. Keep installed Better Auth packages released alongside better-auth on the same release version. Restart pending sign-in and account-linking flows; pre-upgrade state cookies and proxy payloads are rejected. Public options and API signatures are unchanged.WorkaroundsUntil you upgrade to the fixed release, apply one of these:Set one strong OAuth Proxy secret across every environment that takes part in the proxy flow, and keep it different from each environment's global Better Auth secret.Set account.storeStateStrategy: "database". This is already the default when a database or secondary storage is configured. If Magic Link is also enabled, switching can expose a separate cross-purpose verification-record path in affected releases. Ensure the two flows resolve to distinct stored identifiers; with built-in options, use Magic Link storeToken: "hashed" with global verification.storeIdentifier unset or "plain", or disable Magic Link or both built-in social and Generic OAuth sign-in.Remove the OAuth Proxy plugin if you do not need it.Setting account.accountLinking.disableImplicitLinking: true stops this path from taking over an existing account. It does not fix the underlying flaw: the callback can still accept attacker-made data as a provider identity. Apply one of the steps above as well.Referenceshttps://github.com/better-auth/better-auth/security/advisories/GHSA-r4xp-prcw-77qfhttps://github.com/better-auth/better-auth/pull/11494https://github.com/better-auth/better-auth/commit/ac54bfd67821a7607533af2059858b12bc54e26ahttps://github.com/better-auth/better-auth/releases/tag/v1.7.7https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-r4xp-prcw-77qf

items.title: [better-auth] better-auth: OAuth state can be used as a Magic Link to sign in as another user
items.summary: Am I affected?You may be affected if you use better-auth from 1.4.0-beta.18 through versions before 1.7.7 with the Magic Link plugin and social or Generic OAuth sign-in.You are affected if all of these are true:Magic Link is enabled with default storeToken: "plain", or with storeToken: "hashed" and global verification.storeIdentifier: "hashed" (including a hashed default).At least one built-in social provider or Generic OAuth provider is enabled.OAuth state uses account.storeStateStrategy: "database", the default when a database or secondary storage is configured.Cookie-backed state blocks this path, subject to the OAuth Proxy condition below. With custom hashers, confirm the flows cannot resolve to the same stored identifier.SummaryBetter Auth accepts an OAuth sign-in state value as a Magic Link token. An attacker can start an OAuth sign-in with any email address and use the returned state value to finish a Magic Link sign-in for that address. They never prove that they can read that email.ImpactAn unauthenticated attacker who knows a user's email address can get a normal session for that user, with all of that account's permissions. They need no access to the mailbox, and they do not need to sign in with the OAuth provider or complete an OAuth callback.If Magic Link sign-up is enabled and no user has the email address, the attacker can instead create an account that Better Auth wrongly marks as email verified, and is signed in to it. The false verified-email flag can also bypass Better Auth's default unproven-account protections when the mailbox owner later signs in, leaving the attacker's session in that account. Applications that trust verified email addresses or email domains may give this account more access, depending on the application.PatchesThe fix is merged for the planned better-auth 1.7.7 release. That package is not available yet.Upgrade better-auth and installed Better Auth adapters, plugins, and integrations released alongside it together. Upgrade servers sharing verification storage in the same cutover. Request new Magic Links and restart pending OAuth or SAML sign-ins; links and state created before the upgrade cannot complete. Update custom verification.storeIdentifier.overrides rules to match the magic-link: and auth-state: prefixes. There is no user or account data migration, and public token values and API signatures are unchanged.WorkaroundsUntil you upgrade to the fixed release, use one of these mitigations:Set account.storeStateStrategy to "cookie". If you also use OAuth Proxy, first configure one dedicated OAuth Proxy secret across all participating environments that differs from each environment's global Better Auth secret. Cookie-backed state can expose a separate OAuth Proxy account-takeover path when the proxy shares the global secret and implicit account linking is enabled.Set the Magic Link plugin option storeToken to "hashed" and leave global verification.storeIdentifier unset or set it to "plain". Global identifier hashing does not prevent this issue when Magic Link tokens are also hashed.Turn off Magic Link sign-in, or turn off social and Generic OAuth sign-in.Setting disableSignUp: true on the Magic Link plugin is not enough. It only stops the creation of new verified accounts. It does not stop the takeover of existing accounts.Referenceshttps://github.com/better-auth/better-auth/security/advisories/GHSA-965c-763c-88jmhttps://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-114607https://github.com/better-auth/better-auth/pull/11494https://github.com/better-auth/better-auth/commit/ac54bfd67821a7607533af2059858b12bc54e26ahttps://github.com/better-auth/better-auth/releases/tag/v1.7.7https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-965c-763c-88jm

items.title: [nodemailer] Nodemailer: Quadratic backtracking in SMTP AUTH mechanism detection regexes allows pre-auth remote denial of service
[nodemailer] Nodemailer: RFC 5322 comment inside an angle-bracket address is never stripped
items.summary: SummaryNodemailer's address parser has three published, patched fixes for RFC 5322 comment ( ... ) handling inside an addr-spec: GHSA-cc9r-2j5m-2m83 (comment glued two domain atoms into one), GHSA-g57g-f23g-4646 (the same glue for a quoted local part), and the related ReDoS fixes GHSA-prgh-xp8r-p3m5 / GHSA-v53p-9fqp-m79j. All three fixes live in _handleAddress()'s joins / _recoverAddrSpec() logic in src/addressparser/index.ts, and that logic is exercised whenever the local text-accumulation path in the tokenizer runs.That logic is never reached at all for the single most common way a recipient is written: a display name followed by an angle-bracket address, Name <local@domain>. When the input inside the angle brackets itself contains an RFC 5322 comment, e.g.Legit User <user@good-corp.com(x)evil.com>the comment is not recognized as an operator, is not stripped, and the parenthesis characters survive verbatim inside the parsed address. That value is used as-is for envelope.to and is written raw onto the wire in the RCPT TO SMTP command. I confirmed this end to end:against nodemailer's own jsonTransport/streamTransport (envelope.to and the emitted To: header both carry the malformed value), andagainst a real SMTP server (aiosmtpd), where the malformed value is fatal to the transaction (501 Syntax: RCPT TO: <address> [SP <mail-parameters>], all recipients rejected).This reproduces unmodified on every version I tested from 6.9.16 through the current 10.0.12 HEAD, i.e. it predates and survives all three of the address-parser advisories above unchanged, because it is a different root cause in a code path those fixes never touch.Root cause1. The tokenizer has a single-slot operator stacksrc/addressparser/index.ts, Tokenizer.checkChar():} else if (!this.operatorExpecting && !this.inDomainLiteral && chr in this.operators) {    this.node = { type: 'operator', value: chr };    this.list.push(this.node);    this.node = null;    this.operatorExpecting = this.operators[chr];    this.escaped = false;    return;}(currently around line 670)operatorExpecting is a single string, not a stack. Once < opens the address scope, operatorExpecting is set to '>'. The branch above that recognizes a new operator character (such as () is gated on !this.operatorExpecting, which is now false. So while inside <...>, a ( is never tokenized as an operator at all — it is just an ordinary character appended to the running text token, together with everything up to the next >. The RFC 5322 comment is not recognized, not entered, and not stripped: it rides straight through as literal text.2. The _handleAddress state machine loses the address state on any operator boundarysrc/addressparser/index.ts, inside _handleAddress() (currently around line 365-388):switch (token.value) {    case '<':        state = 'address';        insideQuotes = false;        break;    case '(':        state = 'comment';        insideQuotes = false;        break;    ...    default:        state = 'text';        insideQuotes = false;        break;}Even where a comment is recognized (outside angle brackets), closing it with ) falls through to default and resets state to 'text', not back to whatever state was active before the comment opened. This is why the fixed cases (bare address, quoted local part) only work at all: the leaked comment tail lands in the free-text bucket, where _recoverAddrSpec()/the ADDR_SPEC extraction logic can find and strip it. Inside <...>, none of that applies in the first place (point 1), so there is no text-bucket safety net to fall back on — the whole point 1/point 2 interaction is what makes the angle-bracket case categorically different from, and unprotected by, the three existing fixes.3. The one existing safety net requires whitespace, and this value has none_recoverAddrSpec() (currently around line 283) is the function all three prior fixes rely on to peel a clean addr-spec back out of a polluted value. Its very first line is:function _recoverAddrSpec(data: { address: string; text: string }): void {    if (!HAS_WHITESPACE.test(data.address)) {        return;    }    ...user@good-corp.com(x)evil.com contains no whitespace at all — the comment content x had none, and nothing in the angle-bracket path inserts any — so _recoverAddrSpec bails out immediately and never even looks at the value. There is no cleanup path for this shape.Proof of ConceptEnvironment: Node.js, current master (commit 30e4cfd5902fd5da4d1bc76dc8e4bc92d288adef, package.json version 10.0.12), no special transport configuration required.Parser-level confirmationconst addressparser = require('nodemailer/lib/addressparser');console.log(addressparser('Legit User <user@good-corp.com(x)evil.com>'));// [ { address: 'user@good-corp.com(x)evil.com', name: 'Legit User' } ]Compare with the already-fixed, unbracketed form of the exact same bytes:console.log(addressparser('user@good-corp.com(x)evil.com'));// [ { address: 'user@good-corp.com', name: 'evil.com' } ]   <- correctly strippeds

items.title: [nodemailer] Nodemailer: Quadratic (O(n^2)) SMTP client reply parsing lets a malicious server or MITM cause a pre-auth remote denial of service
items.summary:
SummaryThe SMTP client response parser reassembles multiline server replies by appending each continuation line onto a single response-queue entry and re-testing whether that entry is still a partial (continuation) reply on every line. The partial-response test runs str.slice(str.lastIndexOf('
') + 1) on the growing entry, which forces a full flatten of the entire accumulated string on each line. A malicious or compromised SMTP server (or an on-path attacker on a plaintext or pre-STARTTLS hop) that streams continuation lines and never sends a completion line drives O(n^2) CPU on the single-threaded Node.js event loop before any authentication, freezing the whole process for an attacker-controlled duration.Root CauseThe invariant that a server cannot cause superlinear client-side work while a reply is being reassembled is violated. In src/smtp-connection/index.ts, _onData splits inbound bytes into lines and, while the last queued entry is a continuation reply, concatenates each new line onto that same entry with this._responseQueue[len - 1] += '
' + lines[i]. On every iteration it calls isPartialResponse(lastline), which evaluates /^\d+-/.test(str.slice(str.lastIndexOf('
') + 1)). Because the queued entry grows by one line per continuation line and is stored as a V8 rope (ConsString), each lastIndexOf/slice forces a full string flatten of length proportional to the accumulated reply. Executed once per line over n continuation lines, this is O(n^2) CPU. While the reply stays partial the function early-returns and never resets the entry, so the growth and the per-line reflatten continue unbounded. There is no response-size or line-count cap in the connection code; the only limits are time-based (greetingTimeout, and an inactivity socketTimeout), and neither bounds accumulated reply size.Affected file and functions (verified at the published v10.0.9 artifact, in src/ and in the built dist/cjs and dist/esm output):- src/smtp-connection/index.ts: isPartialResponse (the /^\d+-/ test over str.slice(str.lastIndexOf('
')+1))- src/smtp-connection/index.ts: SMTPConnection._onData (the continuation-line append loop with no size cap)ImpactAn attacker who is, or can impersonate, the SMTP peer the client connects to can freeze the connecting Node.js process. Because Node.js is single-threaded, event-loop starvation halts all other work in that process (every other connection, request, and timer), not just the offending SMTP session. The reply is parsed during the greeting and EHLO phases, before the client authenticates or issues any command, so no credentials on the client are required. The blocking duration scales with the volume of continuation data the attacker streams and can be sustained indefinitely by continuing to stream, and memory for the accumulated entry also grows without bound. Independent reproduction on Node.js 24 measured roughly 11.6 seconds of event-loop blocking for about 640 KB of continuation data and roughly 47 seconds for about 1.3 MB, scaling quadratically. This is a repeatable remote denial of service against the sending process.Proof of ConceptNode.js 24; a raw TCP listener acting as a hostile SMTP server; the client uses the shipped SMTPConnection (require('nodemailer/lib/smtp-connection')).Steps: (1) start a TCP server that accepts a connection and streams continuation lines of the form 220-flood...
 in large batches, never emitting a completion line such as 220 ready; (2) point an SMTPConnection at it and observe the client event loop stall while the single response-queue entry grows and is reflattened on every line. A minimal microbenchmark of the exact parsing logic demonstrates the complexity:// Reproduces isPartialResponse + the _onData append loop verbatim (Node 24).function isPartialResponse(str) { return /^\d+-/.test(str.slice(str.lastIndexOf('
') + 1)); }function run(n) {    const queue = [];    let remainder = '';    function onData(chunk) {        const lines = (remainder + chunk).split(/?
/);        remainder = lines.pop();        for (let i = 0; i < lines.length; i++) {            if (queue.length && isPartialResponse(queue[queue.length - 1])) {                queue[queue.length - 1] += '
' + lines[i];                continue;            }            queue.push(lines[i]);        }    }    let buf = '';    for (let i = 0; i < n; i++) buf += '220-flood line ' + i + '
';    const t = Date.now();    onData(buf);    return Date.now() - t;}for (const n of [8000, 16000, 32000, 64000]) console.log(n, run(n) + 'ms');8000   26.5ms16000  357.6ms32000  2712.0ms64000  11645.1ms(2x input yields roughly 4x-7x time: quadratic. ~640 KB of continuation data blocks the event loop ~11.6s.)Attack ChainExposure: The client opens an SMTP connection whose peer is attacker-controlled or attacker-influenced: a compromised or malicious configured server, a tenant-supplied outbound server in a multi-tenant "bring your own SMTP" deployment, a deliverability or mailbox-probing tool that connects

items.title: [better-auth] better-auth: Device login approval does not show the requesting client or permissions
items.summary: Am I affected?You may be affected if you use better-auth from 1.3.8-beta.3 up to, but not including, 1.7.0-rc.3, and you enable the deviceAuthorization() plugin. This range includes all 1.6 releases.You are affected only if all of these are also true:An attacker can start a device request: validateClient is not configured, or the attacker can use a valid public client.Before allowing approval, your approval page does not show, from server-checked data, which client is asking and the exact permissions it requests.Users may approve a code or complete verification link they did not start and cannot compare with a device they have.Your application accepts the session token that the device flow returns, for example through the bearer plugin.You are not affected if you do not enable the opt-in deviceAuthorization() plugin.SummaryThe device authorization plugin lets a user sign in on one device by approving a short code on another. In affected versions, the approval information given to the user leaves out which client asked for access and which permissions it wants. The official approval examples therefore show only a generic request and a code, so users cannot tell their own device from an attacker's request.ImpactAn attacker who convinces a signed-in user to approve the attacker's code receives a live Better Auth session token for that user. The attacker can then read or change any data the user's account can access. The attack needs the opt-in device flow, a request the attacker creates, and a user who actively approves it; it is not a sign-in bypass without user action.PatchesThe fix first shipped in 1.7.0-rc.3. Upgrade to better-auth@1.7.0 or later. No 1.6 release contains the fix.After upgrading, GET /device returns the requesting client_id and scope to the signed-in account that owns the request. If you built your own approval page, update it to show that client and those permissions, and keep approval disabled until they load.WorkaroundsIf you cannot upgrade yet, do the following:Disable deviceAuthorization(), or block untrusted access to /device/code.Configure a strict validateClient allowlist. Do not rely on the allowlist alone: it limits who can start the flow, but it does not give users the missing approval information.Build your own approval endpoint. It should read the pending request from trusted server-side storage and map the checked client identifier to a trusted display name. Show the exact requested permissions and the user code. Keep approval disabled until this information loads.Tell users to reject device requests they did not expect. They should approve only when the same code is visible right now on a device they have.Technical detailsA device starts the flow by calling /device/code. The plugin stores the client identifier and any requested scope with the pending request. Before approval, GET /device returns only the user code and its status. This is true even for a signed-in session of the user account that owns the request. An approval page built from that response cannot show which client asked for access or which permissions it wants. After approval, the original device code can be redeemed at /device/token for a Better Auth session token.RFC 8628 describes this remote phishing scenario. It recommends that the server tell users they are authorizing a device and ask them to confirm that the device is in their possession. It also recommends showing device information that helps users detect impersonation. Client allowlisting reduces who can start the flow, but it does not give users the missing approval information. A valid public client can therefore still be affected when its identifier and requested permissions are not shown.Referenceshttps://github.com/better-auth/better-auth/security/advisories/GHSA-q84f-53jg-9ppmhttps://github.com/better-auth/better-auth/commit/f68044dcfbd9fb83763249ed9509cfacbcce47behttps://github.com/better-auth/better-auth/releases/tag/v1.7.0-rc.3https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-q84f-53jg-9ppm

items.title: [satori] Satori-generated SVG has improper escaping
items.summary: ImpactSatori does not properly escape certain values before including them in generated SVG output. This can allow crafted values to be interpreted as SVG markup.The impact depends on how the generated SVG is consumed.WorkaroundNo complete workaround exists besides upgrading. Applications that cannot immediately upgrade should not render attacker-controlled content with Satori.Referenceshttps://github.com/vercel/next.js/security/advisories/GHSA-vcvr-r3jv-pc5jhttps://github.com/vercel/satori/security/advisories/GHSA-wx4j-mvgx-mqwphttps://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-94545https://github.com/vercel/satori/pull/814https://github.com/vercel/next.js/commit/868fad38690d72088868f299fa2bef339b26838ehttps://github.com/vercel/satori/commit/26a52affc031216fee5882b6e965c8dbc7ac1782https://github.com/vercel/next.js/releases/tag/v16.3.6https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-wx4j-mvgx-mqwp

items.title: [ghost] Ghost: Authorization Bypass in Comment Like Feature
items.summary: ImpactAn input validation issue allowed members to delete comment likes / dislikes that they were not authorized to delete.Vulnerable versionsThis vulnerability is present in Ghost from v5.9.0 up to v6.44.1.Patchesv6.44.1 contains a fix for this issue.How to updateFor self-hosters using Docker, find Docker's official Ghost image here. Updating a Docker-based Ghost instance is documented here.If your Ghost is a Ghost-CLI install see our documentation on updating it to the latest version here.ReferencesGhost thanks Adel Assakaf and Arthur Gurunlian as well as Geoffrey Diederichs of Escape for disclosing this vulnerability responsibly.For more informationIf you have any questions or comments about this advisory, email us at security@ghost.org.Referenceshttps://github.com/TryGhost/Ghost/security/advisories/GHSA-qrh6-cwg3-343xhttps://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-103288https://github.com/TryGhost/Ghost/pull/28297https://github.com/TryGhost/Ghost/commit/405c2623ff9060295d4a87d3a0eb4ef766c8d2d3https://github.com/TryGhost/Ghost/releases/tag/v6.44.1https://www.vulncheck.com/advisories/ghost-5.9.0-before-6.44.1-authorization-bypass-via-comment-likehttps://github.com/advisories/GHSA-qrh6-cwg3-343x

items.title: [dcmjs] dcmjs: DS/IS VALUE REPRESENTATION INPUT VALIDATION BYPASS
items.summary: dcmjs, a JavaScript library for DICOM manipulation used in web-based medicalimaging viewers, contains an input validation bypass in its handling of DS(Decimal String) and IS (Integer String) value representations.The DecimalString and IntegerString classes in ValueRepresentation.js use aregex sanitizer followed by JavaScript's Number() constructor. While the regexstrips direct NaN/Infinity strings, it preserves scientific notation (includingthe 'e' character), enabling:Infinity injection via scientific notation overflow (1e999999)NaN injection via sign-only remnants from stripped inf strings ("-inf" -> "-")IS accepting scientific notation in violation of PS3.5AFFECTED PRODUCTProduct:          dcmjs (JavaScript DICOM manipulation library)Repository:       https://github.com/dcmjs-org/dcmjsnpm:              https://www.npmjs.com/package/dcmjsAffected Versions: < 0.52.0 (patched in 0.52.0, released 2026-05-19)CVE:              CVE-2026-46350 (assigned by GitHub 2026-05-13)CWE:              CWE-20 (Improper Input Validation)CVSS Score:       7.5 (HIGH)CVSS Vector:      CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:N/I:H/A:HMaintainer note:  The CVSS score above is the reporter's assessment; dcmjs rates this low, because malformed input produces NaN/Infinity in values the caller must range-check in any case (both are reachable by other means, and no trust boundary enforced by dcmjs is crossed).DOWNSTREAM IMPACTdcmjs is a foundational library used by:OHIF Viewer (Open Health Imaging Foundation)Cornerstone.js ecosystemDICOMweb client/server implementationsResearch and clinical web-based PACS viewersAny Node.js or browser application parsing DICOM via dcmjsROOT CAUSEIn src/ValueRepresentation.js, both DecimalString and IntegerString use:let returnVal = numberStr.trim().replace(/[^0-9.\\\-+e]/gi, "");return returnVal === "" ? null : Number(returnVal);The regex /[^0-9.\-+e]/gi strips characters NOT in the set {0-9, ., , -, +,e, E}. This provides partial defense: direct "NaN" and "Infinity" strings arestripped to empty/null. However:  (a) Scientific notation is fully preserved because 'e', digits, '+', '-', '.'      all pass the regex. "1e999999" passes intact, and Number("1e999999")      returns JavaScript Infinity.  (b) The string "-inf" is stripped to just "-" (only the minus passes the      regex). Number("-") returns JavaScript NaN.  (c) IntegerString uses the SAME regex/logic as DecimalString, meaning IS      accepts scientific notation ("1e5" -> 100000) in violation of PS3.5      Section 6.2, which restricts IS to characters 0-9, +, -.  (d) No range validation exists for IS values (PS3.5 requires [-2^31, 2^31-1])      or DS values (16-character max, fixed/floating-point only).VULNERABILITY DETAILSAttack Vector 1: Infinity via Scientific Notation OverflowInput:   DS or IS field containing "1e999999"Regex:   Passes (all chars in allowed set)Result:  Number("1e999999") -> InfinityImpact:  Infinity propagates through all downstream arithmeticAttack Vector 2: Negative Infinity via Scientific NotationInput:   DS or IS field containing "-1e999999"Regex:   PassesResult:  Number("-1e999999") -> -InfinityImpact:  Negative Infinity in spatial/dosimetric calculationsAttack Vector 3: NaN via Sign-Only RemnantInput:   DS or IS field containing "-inf"Regex:   Strips to "-"Result:  Number("-") -> NaNImpact:  NaN propagates silently through arithmetic (IEEE 754)Attack Vector 4: NaN via Plus-Only RemnantInput:   DS or IS field containing "+inf"Regex:   Strips to "+"Result:  Number("+") -> NaNImpact:  Same as aboveAttack Vector 5: IS Scientific Notation BypassInput:   IS field containing "1e5"Regex:   PassesResult:  Number("1e5") -> 100000Impact:  Integer fields accept non-integer representation, violating PS3.5Attack Vector 6: IS Extreme OverflowInput:   IS field containing "1e18"Regex:   PassesResult:  Number("1e18") -> 1000000000000000000Impact:  Far exceeds IS range [-2^31, 2^31-1], no bounds checkCLINICAL IMPACTdcmjs is used in web-based DICOM viewers and processing pipelines.Corrupted values affect:PixelSpacing / ImagePositionPatient: Spatial geometry corruption preventsaccurate measurement and registration in web viewersWindowCenter / WindowWidth: Display pipeline corruption makes imagesunreadable (all black or all white)DoseGridScaling / NumberOfFrames: Radiation therapy dose display errorsand denial of service via frame count overflowRescaleSlope / RescaleIntercept: Hounsfield unit conversion producesinvalid values, corrupting quantitative analysisSliceThickness: Volume reconstruction fails in multiplanar
